chapters.title: Chapter 9: Capstone: Running a Market Making Book Through a Volatile Month

lessons.title: Reviewing the Month: What Worked, What Didn't, and What Changes Next

body.text: A month is long enough to finally ask the question Chapter 6 posed at the start: was any of this a genuine edge, or just a lucky stretch that has not yet been tested enough to know?

children.text: Weeks Three and Four: Filling Out the Picture

Week three returns to something close to week one's calm baseline, with one more scheduled event handled cleanly through the same calendar-based playbook. Week four brings a different kind of stress entirely: a sharp USDINR depreciation, driven by the global dynamics covered in Chapter 7, spills over into broad risk-off sentiment that pushes Bank Nifty lower and briefly turns order flow one-sided again. This time, having lived through week two, the desk recognises the pattern faster and manages it with a smaller peak inventory buildup and a noticeably smaller worst-case loss than week two's shock produced.

children.text: Applying Chapter 6's Test One Last Time

Chapter 6 set out exactly what would separate a genuine edge from a lucky stretch: spread capture rate collapsing toward zero or negative under stress, and losses breaching the book's own hard limits. Neither happened this month. Spread capture rate fell meaningfully in both stress weeks, but never dropped below roughly half of its calm-week level. The worst single session, week two's ₹95,000 loss, stayed clearly inside the ₹1.5 lakh kill switch, and the month's largest drawdown of ₹1.4 lakh stayed well inside the ₹5 lakh pause threshold. By Chapter 6's own standard, this month's evidence points toward a genuine, if imperfect, edge, one that degraded under real stress without ever coming apart.

body.text: Notice also that week four's shock, handled with a smaller peak inventory and a smaller loss than week two's, is itself evidence in favour of a genuine, learnable edge, since it shows the desk's judgement improving with direct experience rather than each new shock catching it equally off guard.

children.text: What Should Actually Change Going Into Month Two

body.caption: Concrete changes proposed for next month, and what they draw on

cells: Inventory nearly hit the 300-unit cap before a deliberate unwind began
Add an earlier, semi-automatic escalation trigger around 200 units, rather than relying purely on discretionary judgement near the hard limit
Chapter 3's escalation framework, tightened using this month's own evidence
Holding time rose to ~27 minutes in week two, well above the 15-minute target
Make the inventory limit dynamic, tightening automatically when VPIN is elevated, rather than one static cap at all times
Chapter 6's Little's Law combined with Chapter 4's VPIN
The calendar-based event playbook worked cleanly in both week one and week three
No change; deliberately preserve this part of the system exactly as designed
Week four's cross-asset spillover was handled better once its pattern was recognised from a related market
Add a supplementary early-warning signal from related markets, such as USDINR moves or GIFT Nifty's overnight trading, alongside instrument-specific VPIN

body.title: Why Leave Something Alone?
body.scenario: A new team member reviewing this month's proposed changes questions why the calendar-based event playbook is being left completely unchanged when every other part of the system is being adjusted.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's own review, explain why 'no change' is sometimes the correct output of a serious review, rather than a sign the review wasn't thorough enough.
body.modelAnswer: A review's job is to identify what the evidence actually supports, not to find something to change everywhere for its own sake. The calendar-based event playbook was tested twice this month, in weeks one and three, and both times it performed exactly as intended, with no signs of strain. Changing something that has been genuinely tested and has worked is more likely to introduce new risk than to improve anything, while the other three changes are each responding to a specific, observed weak point, inventory nearly reaching its cap, holding time running longer than intended, and a slower-than-ideal recognition of a cross-asset pattern. A thorough review changes what the evidence says needs changing and explicitly protects what the evidence says is already working.

body.title: The Final Verdict on This Month
body.question: Based on this lesson's application of Chapter 6's framework, what is the most accurate summary verdict on this month's book?
options: No real edge; the calm weeks' good numbers were pure luck that stress fully exposed
A genuine, if imperfect, edge: metrics degraded under real stress without collapsing, losses stayed inside every pre-set limit, and performance improved from week two to week four
The book should be shut down immediately due to excessive risk
The results are inconclusive and no verdict can be drawn from a single month
body.explanation: Chapter 6's specific markers of a lucky, edge-less stretch, spread capture collapsing to near zero or negative and hard limits being breached, did not appear this month. Spread capture rate stayed meaningfully positive even under stress, every loss stayed inside its designed limit, and the desk's handling of week four's shock improved on week two's, all of which point toward a genuine, workable, if imperfect, edge rather than an absence of one.

points: This month's blended numbers, a 74% overall spread capture rate, contained worst-case losses, and a positive net P&L across both calm and volatile weeks, meet Chapter 6's own bar for a genuine, if imperfect, edge

A serious review changes what the evidence says needs changing, the escalation trigger and the static inventory cap here, and explicitly protects what the evidence says already works, the calendar-based event playbook
Performance improving from week two's shock to week four's, rather than staying equally poor, is itself meaningful evidence of a learnable, genuine edge

This capstone has walked one desk through every layer of this course: Chapter 1's basic quoting business, Chapters 2 through 4's spread, inventory, and adverse selection mechanics, Chapter 5's execution and regulatory tools, Chapter 6's evaluation framework, Chapter 7's cross-asset awareness, and Chapter 8's understanding of who does this work and how they get hired

None of these tools function as well in isolation as they do together: a pricing model without risk limits, a risk limit without a metric framework to evaluate it, or a metric framework without the market microstructure understanding to interpret it correctly, would each fall short of what this month's book actually needed

Market making, at its core, remains what Chapter 1 first described: providing liquidity by quoting both sides continuously, earning the spread for doing so, and surviving long enough between calm weeks and volatile ones to let that structural edge actually compound
